speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. To help diagnose your condition, could you describe the skin lesions in detail and tell me when the fever and wrist pain started?

speaker: Patient
text: 17-year-old male. The patient presents with a 3-day history of pain in his left wrist, which worsened this morning accompanied by chills and malaise. He recounts having a self-resolving left knee pain the previous week. Reports recent return from a camping trip in Minnesota. Sexually active with one female partner. No history of trauma to the wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text: Did you notice any tick bites or a spreading "bull's-eye" rash on your skin during or after your camping trip? Have you experienced any headache, stiff neck, or facial drooping?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Pain in the left wrist. I also have Chills, Malaise, Painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on both wrists and hands, Swelling and erythema of the left wrist, Severe tenderness to palpation and passive movement of the left wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text: The painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on your hands and wrists, combined with the monoarticular arthritis and recent camping in Minnesota, are highly suggestive of a specific tick-borne illness. Do you recall seeing any ticks on your body during or after your trip, and have you noticed any joint pain in other areas besides the knee and wrist? REQUEST TEST: PCR for Ehrlichia and Anaplasma

speaker: Doctor
text: The negative PCR results for Ehrlichia and Anaplasma make those diagnoses unlikely, so I need to focus on the distinctive skin lesions and arthritis. REQUEST TEST: Serology for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever and Lyme disease.

speaker: Doctor
text: The negative serology for RMSF and Lyme, combined with the specific violaceous vesiculopustular lesions and history of camping in Minnesota, strongly points toward a different tick-borne pathogen. REQUEST TEST: Serology for Ehrlichia chaffeensis and Anaplasma phagocytophilum.

speaker: Doctor
text: The negative results for Ehrlichia and Anaplasma, along with the distinctive painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on the extremities following a camping trip in Minnesota, are classic for Boutonneuse fever or a similar spotted fever group rickettsiosis, but the geography and lesion type strongly suggest Tularemia or potentially a rare presentation of another rickettsial disease. Given the specific lesion description and location, I am considering Tularemia (ulceroglandular or typhoidal form with skin involvement) or perhaps a misidentified RMSF variant, but let's look for direct evidence. REQUEST TEST: Serology for Francisella tularensis and Rickettsia rickettsia.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the classic presentation of fever, arthritis, and painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on the extremities after camping in Minnesota, this is highly characteristic of Southern Tick-Associated Rash Illness (STARI) or, more likely, a specific rickettsial infection like Ehrlichiosis that may have been missed by initial serology. I will request a blood smear to look for morulae in white blood cells, which is diagnostic for Ehrlichiosis. REQUEST TEST: Peripheral blood smear

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Peripheral blood smear: No morulae identified in white blood cells.

speaker: Doctor
text: The negative tests for common tick-borne illnesses and the specific description of painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on the hands and wrists, combined with fever and monoarticular arthritis, are highly suggestive of Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, despite the initial negative serology which can be false-negative in early disease. I will request a skin biopsy of one of the lesions for immunohistochemical staining to confirm the diagnosis. REQUEST TEST: Skin biopsy with immunohistochemistry for Rickettsia rickettsia

speaker: Doctor
text: With all standard tick-borne serologies and biopsies negative, the presence of painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on the extremities alongside fever and arthritis in a young male strongly suggests Disseminated Gonococcal Infection. I will request a PCR test on the wrist joint fluid and a NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. REQUEST TEST: Joint fluid PCR for Neisseria gonorrhoeae

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Joint aspiration: Gram-negative diplococci seen; STI Screen: Gonorrhea Positive

speaker: Doctor
text: The presence of Gram-negative diplococci in the joint fluid and a positive gonorrhea screen confirms the diagnosis. DIAGNOSIS READY: Disseminated Gonococcal Infection
